[G00001]  OK, let's start with the Mandel Fleming mold.
 Now, this is a mold that I think is extremely useful.
 And in the short term, it will be important for you
 because probably 70% of the quiz will be related to things
 that are too small, meaning we're
 going to use this mold for different things.
 But if you understand it well, you probably
 have 70% of the last quiz under control.
 So I'm going to go very slowly over it and please stop me if there's any step you don't
 understand.
 I put steps into myself so I don't rush because, again, I think it's important to understand
 things.
 So here you have the exchange rate, two exchange rates.
 The white one is the euro-dollar exchange rate.
 I'm quoting it the opposite of the way it's normally quoted.
 There are some conventions in FX markets,
 but this is, as we have defined in this course,
 is if it goes up, it means an appreciation
 of a local currency, that is, the dollar.

[G00002]  That is, you get more of the foreign currency
 per unit of the domestic currency when it goes up.
 And down is a depreciation.
 And you see there that this is the dollar
 became gain value relative to the euro through all this period.
 And then he has lost quite a bit of value since sort of late 2022.
 With respect to the Japanese yen, that's the blue line,
 it was the whole cycle is even more dramatic.
 Big appreciation of the dollar, depreciation of the yen,
 and a reversal since late 2022 and so on.
 So, what is behind these big fluctuations?
 Many things, effects are volatile, like almost any asset price.
 But one of the main drivers of these fluctuations is perceptions about interest rate policy
 in the different parts of the world.
 So the reason we have seen a lot of this decline here, so the reason for the rise here
 of the dollar is mostly because investors in general
 perceived that the US was more advanced in its business
 cycle.

[G00003]  It began to tighten interest rates
 before the rest of the world.
 And since interest rates were rising in the US,
 that led to an appreciation of the dollar
 by a mechanism they described at the end
 of the previous lecture.
 But I'm going to repeat today.
 Remember when I talked about the uncovering
 interest-party condition, what is related
 to what I'm talking about here.
 And I'm going to, again, go again over that.
 And a big reason for the decline, more recently,
 is simply that there is a sense that monetary policy is
 speaking in the US in terms of tightness,
 while the rest of the world is catching up.
 And in the case of Europe, more than catching up
 because they have further supply shocks coming
 from energy shocks and so on.
 So you look, for example, at the expected policy rate path
 In the case of the US nowadays, it looks like this.
 So the steel market expects some hikes in the US,
 but a limited amount of hikes.

[G00004]  And then they expect quickly the Fed to start undoing that.
 That's what this path is telling you.
 This is a expected policy rate path.
 What the market thinks now, the policy rate
 will be in the next meeting, two meetings from now,
 three meetings from now, four meetings of the FOMC from now.
 Well, if you look at the same picture in Europe,
 it looks like that.
 It's clear that there is more ahead.
 And you see that's what the market perceived at this point.
 Whether that ends up being true or not doesn't matter.
 At any point in time, the exchanges
 determine where the markets think.
 So what actually happens is less important for an asset price.
 An asset price is a lot about pricing today,
 things that you expect to happen in the future.
 What you expect is what matters, not what
 actually happens, and at this moment,
 the market expects the euro area to go
 through a more prolonged period of hiking, interest rate
 hiking.

 Now, this is a mold that I think is extremely useful.
 And in the short term, it will be important for you
 because probably 70% of the quiz will be related to things
 that are too small, meaning we're
 going to use this mold for different things.
 But if you understand it well, you probably
 have 70% of the last quiz under control.
 So I'm going to go very slowly over it and please stop me if there's any step you don't
 understand.
 I put steps into myself so I don't rush because, again, I think it's important to understand
 things.
 So here you have the exchange rate, two exchange rates.
 The white one is the euro-dollar exchange rate.
 I'm quoting it the opposite of the way it's normally quoted.
 There are some conventions in FX markets,
 but this is, as we have defined in this course,
 is if it goes up, it means an appreciation
 of a local currency, that is, the dollar.

[G00002]  That is, you get more of the foreign currency
 per unit of the domestic currency when it goes up.
 And down is a depreciation.
 And you see there that this is the dollar
 became gain value relative to the euro through all this period.
 And then he has lost quite a bit of value since sort of late 2022.
 With respect to the Japanese yen, that's the blue line,
 it was the whole cycle is even more dramatic.
 Big appreciation of the dollar, depreciation of the yen,
 and a reversal since late 2022 and so on.
 So, what is behind these big fluctuations?
 Many things, effects are volatile, like almost any asset price.
 But one of the main drivers of these fluctuations is perceptions about interest rate policy
 in the different parts of the world.
 So the reason we have seen a lot of this decline here, so the reason for the rise here
 of the dollar is mostly because investors in general
 perceived that the US was more advanced in its business
 cycle.

[G00003]  It began to tighten interest rates
 before the rest of the world.
 And since interest rates were rising in the US,
 that led to an appreciation of the dollar
 by a mechanism they described at the end
 of the previous lecture.
 But I'm going to repeat today.
 Remember when I talked about the uncovering
 interest-party condition, what is related
 to what I'm talking about here.
 And I'm going to, again, go again over that.
 And a big reason for the decline, more recently,
 is simply that there is a sense that monetary policy is
 speaking in the US in terms of tightness,
 while the rest of the world is catching up.
 And in the case of Europe, more than catching up
 because they have further supply shocks coming
 from energy shocks and so on.
 So you look, for example, at the expected policy rate path
 In the case of the US nowadays, it looks like this.
 So the steel market expects some hikes in the US,
 but a limited amount of hikes.

[G00004]  And then they expect quickly the Fed to start undoing that.
 That's what this path is telling you.
 This is a expected policy rate path.
 What the market thinks now, the policy rate
 will be in the next meeting, two meetings from now,
 three meetings from now, four meetings of the FOMC from now.
 Well, if you look at the same picture in Europe,
 it looks like that.
 It's clear that there is more ahead.
 And you see that's what the market perceived at this point.
 Whether that ends up being true or not doesn't matter.
 At any point in time, the exchanges
 determine where the markets think.
 So what actually happens is less important for an asset price.
 An asset price is a lot about pricing today,
 things that you expect to happen in the future.
 What you expect is what matters, not what
 actually happens, and at this moment,
 the market expects the euro area to go
 through a more prolonged period of hiking, interest rate
 hiking.

[G00005]  Japan hasn't had hikes in interest rates for three
 decades, but even now, you begin to see some.
 The scale here is very small.
 These are a few basis points.
 But even the point I'm trying to make
 is that certainly people expect interest rates in the US
 has to go down relative to interest rates in Japan.
 Not to say that the interest rate in the US
 will be lower than the interest rate in Japan,
 but the direction of the change is in that way.
 So relative to where we're at now,
 the direction of the change is towards the US loosening
 monetary policy before the rest of the world does.
 And that's what is leading to its big swings.
 Say before, this is a period in which the US had
 to start tightening before the rest and the currency
 opportunity a lot, especially with respect to the yen,
 because again, the yen has been against the zero
 overbound for a very long time.

[G00006]  So nobody expected the yen to move, to follow the US.
 And while with respect to Europe,
 well, Europe was having inflationary problems
 and so on as well, so people expected it
 to follow the US at some point.
 For Japan, there was nothing like that.
 And that's what led to the massive depreciation
 of the gain, appreciation of the US dollar vis-a-vis again.
 So what the Mandela Fleming model is about,
 it's about first connecting these things,
 trying to understand what moves the exchange rate, how
 different monetary policies in different places,
 or different policies in different places in the world,
 affect exchange rate.
 And then it's about understanding
 how those exchange rate movements affect
 real activity in the short run.
 That's what the Mandela Fleming model is.
 So it is really, we're gonna go back to our old ISLM model,
 very short run, we're gonna even fix
 nominal prices and so on.
 So back to that environment,
 but we're gonna do it in an open economy,
 so we're gonna have a new variable floating around,
 which is the exchange rate,
 and we need to understand how the exchange rate moves
 when different things happen in different countries,
 and what is the impact of that on aggregate demand,
 and hence on output, we're talking about the very short run,
 in the different parts of the world.

[G00007]  So that's a plan.
 That's what we intend to do.
 So let's start with this Mandel Fleming model.
 Remember, we wrote down the equilibrium in the goods market
 in the previous lecture.
 And I'm just reproducing what I wrote in the previous lecture.
 So it looks exactly like the close economy output
 is being determined by already demand.
 But it's already demand for domestically produced goods.
 domestic reduced goods is not the same as domestic demand for goods, which is this,
 because now there's a net export term. So part of the things that the residents sort of demand,
 they demand from the rest of the world, not from domestic producers, and at the same time part of
 the demand perceived by domestic producers comes from the rest of the world, from exports, not from
 domestic producers. So that's the reason we got an extra term here, which is this net exports.
 And we said this net exports is a function of three things.

[G00008]  It's a function of output, and it's a decreasing
 function of output.
 Why is that?
 Of domestic output.
 Domestic output, domestic income.
 Why is it a decreasing function of domestic income?
 Why do net exports decline when domestic income rises?
 They import more.
 They consume everything more, but part of that is import.
 And so part of that energy of an extra demand goes to foreign goods and that's what deteriorates net exports, okay?
 And that's the reason we said, how do we just stop there, make the net export function just a function of output
 We would have not needed all these extra paratus
 I'm about to build because all that would have meant is that just we have a smaller multiplier
 It would have been exactly the same as we did in the closed economy
 But with a smaller multiplier because you know every time output goes up now part of that demand goes to
 foreign goods rather than domestic goods.

[G00006]  So nobody expected the yen to move, to follow the US.
 And while with respect to Europe,
 well, Europe was having inflationary problems
 and so on as well, so people expected it
 to follow the US at some point.
 For Japan, there was nothing like that.
 And that's what led to the massive depreciation
 of the gain, appreciation of the US dollar vis-a-vis again.
 So what the Mandela Fleming model is about,
 it's about first connecting these things,
 trying to understand what moves the exchange rate, how
 different monetary policies in different places,
 or different policies in different places in the world,
 affect exchange rate.
 And then it's about understanding
 how those exchange rate movements affect
 real activity in the short run.
 That's what the Mandela Fleming model is.
 So it is really, we're gonna go back to our old ISLM model,
 very short run, we're gonna even fix
 nominal prices and so on.
 So back to that environment,
 but we're gonna do it in an open economy,
 so we're gonna have a new variable floating around,
 which is the exchange rate,
 and we need to understand how the exchange rate moves
 when different things happen in different countries,
 and what is the impact of that on aggregate demand,
 and hence on output, we're talking about the very short run,
 in the different parts of the world.

[G00007]  So that's a plan.
 That's what we intend to do.
 So let's start with this Mandel Fleming model.
 Remember, we wrote down the equilibrium in the goods market
 in the previous lecture.
 And I'm just reproducing what I wrote in the previous lecture.
 So it looks exactly like the close economy output
 is being determined by already demand.
 But it's already demand for domestically produced goods.
 domestic reduced goods is not the same as domestic demand for goods, which is this,
 because now there's a net export term. So part of the things that the residents sort of demand,
 they demand from the rest of the world, not from domestic producers, and at the same time part of
 the demand perceived by domestic producers comes from the rest of the world, from exports, not from
 domestic producers. So that's the reason we got an extra term here, which is this net exports.
 And we said this net exports is a function of three things.

[G00008]  It's a function of output, and it's a decreasing
 function of output.
 Why is that?
 Of domestic output.
 Domestic output, domestic income.
 Why is it a decreasing function of domestic income?
 Why do net exports decline when domestic income rises?
 They import more.
 They consume everything more, but part of that is import.
 And so part of that energy of an extra demand goes to foreign goods and that's what deteriorates net exports, okay?
 And that's the reason we said, how do we just stop there, make the net export function just a function of output
 We would have not needed all these extra paratus
 I'm about to build because all that would have meant is that just we have a smaller multiplier
 It would have been exactly the same as we did in the closed economy
 But with a smaller multiplier because you know every time output goes up now part of that demand goes to
 foreign goods rather than domestic goods.

[G00009]  But it's not so.
 First, because we have another income that matters here,
 which is the income of the rest of the world,
 but more important because we also have an exchange.
 But let's start from this side.
 So net exports is increasing in the income
 of the rest of the world.
 Why is that?
 That is demand for domestically produced goods
 rises when foreign income goes up.
 for an output for an income goes up.
 Why is that?
 It's a symmetric argument, no?
 If with imports, well, our exports
 are the imports of the other country.
 So if the income in the other country goes up,
 then their imports will go up, which
 is our exports that go up.
 That's the reason that exports goes up.
 And the last term, remember, says
 that net exports is declining on the real exchange rate. Why is that? What happens when
 the real exchange rate goes up? It makes our goods more expensive relative to foreign goods.

[G00010]  Exactly. Our goods become more expensive relative to foreign goods, and that affects us from two
 dimensions. First, our exports will tend to decline because our goods are more expensive,
 and also our imports are going to tend to increase because foreign goods are cheaper,
 And so that's the reason this is decreasing with respect to the exchange rate.
 The big thing of the Mandel Fleming model really comes from the fact that this guy is
 there.
 Had we not had the exchange rate there, again, we could have used exactly the same apparatus
 as we used earlier on, but we're going to have an exchange rate floating around, and
 that will require us to build more, a little more.
 We need an extra equation, you know, because we have an extra endogenous variable.
 Now, what I'm going to assume here, as we did in the first part of the course, is that
 both the domestic and foreign prices are completely fixed.

[G00011]  So I'm going to ignore Phillips curve, inflation, expected inflation, and all that.
 I'm going to assume that is zero.
 Expected inflation, inflation, zero.
 When I do that, the same equation, the equilibrium in the goods markets changes a little bit.
 I mean, it's the same equation, but now I don't need to differentiate between real
 interest rate and nominal interest rate,
 because inflation is zero.
 So nominal interest is equal to the real interest rate.
 So I'm going to stick in here the nominal interest rate.
 Second, I really don't need to differentiate
 between real exchange rate and nominal exchange rate,
 because the prices themselves are not changing.
 And so all that will move the real exchange rate
 is the nominal exchange rate.
 So as a reason, I'm going to write here
 that the nominal exchange rate is
 because it's the only thing that will move this variable around,
 given the price that I fixed.
 So that's our equilibrium in the goods market.

[G00012]  And this is a thing you need to compare with lecture 3
 or something like that.
 And as I said, this part here only
 lowers the multipliers, so not a big change.
 This one here is an extra parameter
 that shifts the aggregate demand up and down.
 So you can treat it almost like we treated C0.
 Remember, if the consumer confidence goes up,
 then aggregate demand goes up.
 Well, here we have sort of the rest of the wall's output
 goes up.
 It does exactly the same, the same analysis.
 The problem we have, though, is that we have an extra variable
 here, which is the exchange rate,
 and that's an endogenous variable.
 So we're going to have to come up with some other equation
 to solve for that equation here.
 In lecture three or four, where we did this,
 OK, we said we have two endogenous variables,
 output and the interest rate.
 We need one more equation, while the other equation
 was just monetary policy that set the nominal interest rate.

[G00009]  But it's not so.
 First, because we have another income that matters here,
 which is the income of the rest of the world,
 but more important because we also have an exchange.
 But let's start from this side.
 So net exports is increasing in the income
 of the rest of the world.
 Why is that?
 That is demand for domestically produced goods
 rises when foreign income goes up.
 for an output for an income goes up.
 Why is that?
 It's a symmetric argument, no?
 If with imports, well, our exports
 are the imports of the other country.
 So if the income in the other country goes up,
 then their imports will go up, which
 is our exports that go up.
 That's the reason that exports goes up.
 And the last term, remember, says
 that net exports is declining on the real exchange rate. Why is that? What happens when
 the real exchange rate goes up? It makes our goods more expensive relative to foreign goods.

[G00010]  Exactly. Our goods become more expensive relative to foreign goods, and that affects us from two
 dimensions. First, our exports will tend to decline because our goods are more expensive,
 and also our imports are going to tend to increase because foreign goods are cheaper,
 And so that's the reason this is decreasing with respect to the exchange rate.
 The big thing of the Mandel Fleming model really comes from the fact that this guy is
 there.
 Had we not had the exchange rate there, again, we could have used exactly the same apparatus
 as we used earlier on, but we're going to have an exchange rate floating around, and
 that will require us to build more, a little more.
 We need an extra equation, you know, because we have an extra endogenous variable.
 Now, what I'm going to assume here, as we did in the first part of the course, is that
 both the domestic and foreign prices are completely fixed.

[G00011]  So I'm going to ignore Phillips curve, inflation, expected inflation, and all that.
 I'm going to assume that is zero.
 Expected inflation, inflation, zero.
 When I do that, the same equation, the equilibrium in the goods markets changes a little bit.
 I mean, it's the same equation, but now I don't need to differentiate between real
 interest rate and nominal interest rate,
 because inflation is zero.
 So nominal interest is equal to the real interest rate.
 So I'm going to stick in here the nominal interest rate.
 Second, I really don't need to differentiate
 between real exchange rate and nominal exchange rate,
 because the prices themselves are not changing.
 And so all that will move the real exchange rate
 is the nominal exchange rate.
 So as a reason, I'm going to write here
 that the nominal exchange rate is
 because it's the only thing that will move this variable around,
 given the price that I fixed.
 So that's our equilibrium in the goods market.

[G00012]  And this is a thing you need to compare with lecture 3
 or something like that.
 And as I said, this part here only
 lowers the multipliers, so not a big change.
 This one here is an extra parameter
 that shifts the aggregate demand up and down.
 So you can treat it almost like we treated C0.
 Remember, if the consumer confidence goes up,
 then aggregate demand goes up.
 Well, here we have sort of the rest of the wall's output
 goes up.
 It does exactly the same, the same analysis.
 The problem we have, though, is that we have an extra variable
 here, which is the exchange rate,
 and that's an endogenous variable.
 So we're going to have to come up with some other equation
 to solve for that equation here.
 In lecture three or four, where we did this,
 OK, we said we have two endogenous variables,
 output and the interest rate.

 interest rate and nominal interest rate,
 because inflation is zero.

 So I'm going to stick in here the nominal interest rate.
 Second, I really don't need to differentiate
 between real exchange rate and nominal exchange rate,
 because the prices themselves are not changing.
 And so all that will move the real exchange rate
 is the nominal exchange rate.
 So as a reason, I'm going to write here
 that the nominal exchange rate is
 because it's the only thing that will move this variable around,
 given the price that I fixed.

[G00013]  Here, that's not going to be enough,
 because we also have an exchange rate floating around.
 And we need to bring another equation here
 to deal with this new endogenous variable.
 What is that extra equation?
 Well, it's the uncovered interest parity condition.
 Remember, it's the last expression
 we have in the previous lecture, that takes this form.
 It says, before I simplify lots of things, I wrote this down.
 And it says that the exchange rate is equal to that.
 Now, where does this equation come from?
 What is it trying to do?
 Remember, we talk about this in the context and say, well,
 when you open goods markets, then you
 need a relative price to decide what you're going to buy.
 That's what the real exchanges did.
 And now, then we open the capital account,
 and then people need to decide where
 they're going to invest their money.
 And that equation was related to that.
 But the expected rate of return
 has to be the same for like domestic goods.

[G00014]  Exactly.
 It's what equalizes the expected rate of return.
 In equilibrium, that has to happen.
 Again, in reality, there is risk adjustment.
 There is lots of other factors that we're removing from here.
 But absent those other factors, the returns
 have to be similar in both places.
 Because if one asset is given more return than the other,
 expected return, then people are going
 to invest all of the portfolios in that asset.
 What happens is those flows that
 try to go to those assets that give the highest return
 end up equalizing expected return in equilibrium.
 And that's the equation that does that, exactly that.
 How do I know that?
 Well, remember, I can divide this
 by the exchange rate on both sides.
 And then what you get is 1 equal to a numerator that
 has the nominal exchange rate times the expected appreciation

[G00013]  Here, that's not going to be enough,
 because we also have an exchange rate floating around.
 And we need to bring another equation here
 to deal with this new endogenous variable.
 What is that extra equation?
 Well, it's the uncovered interest parity condition.
 Remember, it's the last expression
 we have in the previous lecture, that takes this form.
 It says, before I simplify lots of things, I wrote this down.
 And it says that the exchange rate is equal to that.
 Now, where does this equation come from?
 What is it trying to do?
 Remember, we talk about this in the context and say, well,
 when you open goods markets, then you
 need a relative price to decide what you're going to buy.
 That's what the real exchanges did.
 And now, then we open the capital account,
 and then people need to decide where
 they're going to invest their money.
 And that equation was related to that.
 But the expected rate of return
 has to be the same for like domestic goods.

[G00014]  Exactly.
 It's what equalizes the expected rate of return.
 In equilibrium, that has to happen.
 Again, in reality, there is risk adjustment.
 There is lots of other factors that we're removing from here.
 But absent those other factors, the returns
 have to be similar in both places.
 Because if one asset is given more return than the other,
 expected return, then people are going
 to invest all of the portfolios in that asset.
 What happens is those flows that
 try to go to those assets that give the highest return
 end up equalizing expected return in equilibrium.
 And that's the equation that does that, exactly that.
 How do I know that?
 Well, remember, I can divide this
 by the exchange rate on both sides.
 And then what you get is 1 equal to a numerator that
 has the nominal exchange rate times the expected appreciation
 of the currency plus.
 And in the denominator, you have the foreign interest rate.
 And so when you compare the two,
 you have to compare one base interest rate, the domestic
 of the foreign, plus expected appreciation
 of the appreciation of that currency.

chunk.text_content:
[G00015]  And that's what this term is doing here, this divided.
 Good.
 So what do we get out of this?
 One thing we're going to do for quite a while,
 because it will simplify things a lot,
 but sometimes also lead to confusion in the way
 we understand why currencies depreciate or appreciate.
 But we'll pause.
 And I'll remind you of this repeatedly.
 We're going to assume for now that the expected exchange
 rate for t plus 1 is fixed.
 And until I tell you otherwise, we're
 going to make this assumption.
 Now, that's a huge simplification,
 completely unrealistic, and so on.
 But it will help me explain the mechanism.
 I mean, one of the things that moves exchanges a lot
 is that people have lots of expectations
 about future exchange rate.
 We'll get to that later.
 But for now, so you understand the mechanism,
 how the Mandel Fleming model works,
 I'm going to assume that we all know
 what the spectral exchange rate, we all
 have a common spectral exchange rate, and it's fixed.

[G00016]  We may move it as a parameter, but I'm
 going to say I'm not going to endogenize that.
 I'm going to take it as fixed, and I
 may move it around to show you what happens when that changes,
 but I'm not going to endogenize it.
 OK, otherwise, I need more equations.
 One more, I want to stop this sequence of equations
 that I would have to build.
 But later, we'll understand more of that, what I just said.
 But for now, just take this as fixed.
 So if I take this as fixed, now I have an equation.
 Remember, I was looking for an equation here
 for my exchange rate.
 Once I do that, then I have what I want.
 I have an equation for my exchange rate today.
 It's just a function of domestic interest rate,
 international interest rate, and the expected exchange rate.
 So I know the following, for example.
 I know that an increase in the domestic interest rate,
 other things equal, appreciates exchange rate.

[G00017]  I can see it in the equation.
 If I move the domestic interest rate up,
 the exchange rate goes up.
 That's an appreciation.
 The dollar becomes more expensive, even simpler.
 Suppose we start with a situation in which the domestic and the international interest rate were the same.
 And now I increase the international interest rate.
 And I'm saying the exchange rate will appreciate.
 Well, first of all, let me start with something even simpler.
 Suppose that this interest rate is equal to international interest rate before analyzing the change I'm about to analyze.
 Then from this equation, what do I know about exchange rate?
 What is it equal to?
 If the domestic interest rate is equal to international interest rate,
 what is the exchange rate today equal to?
 The expected exchange rate of next year, if I have the same interest rates,
 I cannot expect a capital gain or loss from the currency position,
 because I have already an equal interest rate in the two bonds.

[G00018]  So then I'm stuck in a situation where the current exchange rate is
 equal to expected exchange rate, and these two are equal.
 And now I'm going to increase the interest rate, the domestic interest
 rate. And it's very easy for you to read from here that the exchange rate will go up. The
 currency will appreciate. Why? This is not an easy thing to answer unless you know where,
 unless you have read the book or something. That money is only related to the mechanism
 we use to increase interest rate. But I'm saying just use that equation and the logic
 behind that equation, the uncovered interest parity.
 Why is it that if I, you know, we went to a
 transportation which interests me were the same,
 now I increase the domestic interest rate,
 I'm saying the change it has to appreciate.
 No, no, but that's a description of, yeah,
 we know that.
 The question is, what, what is the logic?

[G00019]  Yeah, we know the result.
 What I'm asking is for an economic explanation
 for that result.
 What would I invest in the currency,
 that we need the currency, so the demand is involved
 in something?
 Well, if you go to Wall Street, they
 will explain it in those terms.
 It's not the right explanation, but they will explain it
 in those terms.
 And there is some logic behind that,
 because this equation assumes that the arbitrage happens
 instantaneously.
 Immediately, things move.
 But before that happens, some people
 will start did buy more of the one that has more return.
 But this equation already solved all that.
 And that's when this assumption matters
 and it's a little annoying.
 It bothers me for a lot of reasons,
 but we're going to use it to understand the mechanism.
 You see, if I keep the exchange rate fixed,
 we started with a situation where the exchange rate was
 equal to the expected exchange rate.

[G00020]  If I keep it fixed and I appreciate the currency today,
 then what do I expect to happen to the dollar, let's
 talk about the dollar, from this period to the next one?
 We start from a situation where the exchange rate was
 equal to the expected exchange rate.
 Now I increase the interest rate,
 and I said the exchange rate appreciate.
 Then what do you expect the exchange rate
 to do over the next period?
 If I haven't moved with respect to the exchange rate,
 and now the exchange rate move above the expected exchange
 rate, what do you expect the exchange rate to do?
 Exactly, it has to depreciate.
 So the reason the appreciation happens here
 is because you need to expect to depreciate the dollar
 from this period to the next one.
 Why do I need to expect the exchange rate to depreciate?
 So I'm not appreciating the currency
 because in equilibrium, I need to expect to depreciate.

 equal to expected exchange rate, and these two are equal.

 currency will appreciate. Why? This is not an easy thing to answer unless you know where,

 we use to increase interest rate. But I'm saying just use that equation and the logic
 behind that equation, the uncovered interest parity.

 transportation which interests me were the same,
 now I increase the domestic interest rate,
 I'm saying the change it has to appreciate.

 we know that.

chunk.text_content:
[G00019]  Yeah, we know the result.
 What I'm asking is for an economic explanation
 for that result.
 What would I invest in the currency,
 that we need the currency, so the demand is involved
 in something?
 Well, if you go to Wall Street, they
 will explain it in those terms.
 It's not the right explanation, but they will explain it
 in those terms.
 And there is some logic behind that,
 because this equation assumes that the arbitrage happens
 instantaneously.
 Immediately, things move.
 But before that happens, some people
 will start did buy more of the one that has more return.
 But this equation already solved all that.
 And that's when this assumption matters
 and it's a little annoying.
 It bothers me for a lot of reasons,
 but we're going to use it to understand the mechanism.
 You see, if I keep the exchange rate fixed,
 we started with a situation where the exchange rate was
 equal to the expected exchange rate.

[G00020]  If I keep it fixed and I appreciate the currency today,
 then what do I expect to happen to the dollar, let's
 talk about the dollar, from this period to the next one?
 We start from a situation where the exchange rate was
 equal to the expected exchange rate.
 Now I increase the interest rate,
 and I said the exchange rate appreciate.
 Then what do you expect the exchange rate
 to do over the next period?
 If I haven't moved with respect to the exchange rate,
 and now the exchange rate move above the expected exchange
 rate, what do you expect the exchange rate to do?
 Exactly, it has to depreciate.
 So the reason the appreciation happens here
 is because you need to expect to depreciate the dollar
 from this period to the next one.
 Why do I need to expect the exchange rate to depreciate?
 So I'm not appreciating the currency
 because in equilibrium, I need to expect to depreciate.

[G00021]  That is, I need to expect to lose money
 on the currency part of the trade.
 Why is that?
 Confusion is good, you learn from that.
 And this can be very confusing, I know.
 What is this equation trying to do?
 We are trying to make the specter returns the same.
 That's the whole idea of this.
 So if I am now telling you that one bond is paying a higher interest than the other one,
 I need to offset that somehow. How do I offset it by expecting a depreciation of the bond that is
 denominated in the currency that is expected to depreciate? So what I need to do is compensate
 say, for the interest rate differential
 with an expected depreciation of the currency that's
 paying a higher interest rate.
 So that's what, in this model, when
 I fix the expected exchange rate,
 the only way I can do that is by appreciating the currency today
 so I can expect it to depreciate in the future.

[G00022]  That's the logic.
 Now, what is the connection with what
 in Wall Street they will tell you is to say, well,
 before this may happen not instantaneously.
 It happens somewhat slowly.
 So traders immediately will go to the US dollar bond,
 because they see that they have a higher return.
 And it will be the case until the currency really appreciates.
 Once the currency appreciates enough,
 then that advantage disappears.
 That's what this condition is doing.
 It's making the expected return the same.
 But in the process of the exchange
 of going from the initial exchange
 rate to the new equilibrium exchange rate,
 there may be an opportunity there.
 And that's when you start seeing these flows.
 works.
 That happens very, very fast, but that's
 when you can see some of those flows.
 I mean, in this market, that happens very, very quickly.
 So what is typically wrong is that then an analyst
 comes and tells you, explains the story,
 why the changes, if you want to continue to appreciate,
 well, that's just way too late.

[G00023]  You're already in this environment.
 You lost the trade.
 What about an increase in the foreign interest rate,
 i star?
 So an increase in the foreign interest rate,
 let's start from the same situation we had before.
 We start from interest rate equal to international interest
 rate, therefore, the exchange rate
 is equal to expected exchange rate.
 And now, the foreign interest rate goes up.
 What is going on now in the US?
 The US is sort of stabilizing here,
 and Europe is beginning to hike a little more than the US.
 So we know from the equation that that means the exchange
 rate will fall, that is, will drop here.
 So that means the exchange rate is depreciating.
 and the dollar is depreciating.
 Why is the dollar depreciating?
 Yeah, that's correct.
 I mean, the issue here in terms of the economics
 is that, remember, if we start from the same interest rate
 and now all the lines that I'm giving you
 doesn't need to start from the same interest rate.

[G00024]  It's simpler to start from the same interest.
 But suppose we start with the same interest rate
 and now we increase this one, then
 that means the foreign bond is playing a higher interest
 rate than the domestic bond.
 I need to equalize the expected returns.
 The only way I can do that is by having an expected
 appreciation of the dollar.
 Since the expected exchange, if we fix it here, the only way
 I can give you an expected appreciation of the dollar is
 by depreciating the dollar today.
 So it's the same mechanism, the same logic, it's symmetric.
 That's the mechanism.
 Now, is this true in the very short run?
 When i star goes up and i doesn't move, then lots of
 People go and buy foreign bonds, and that produces demand
 for euros and blah, blah, blah, blah.
 But that's very quick.
 Machines do it for you now.
 It happens very quickly.
 So this equation shows you what happens after all that mess
 has already clear, which happens in milliseconds now.

[G00021]  That is, I need to expect to lose money
 on the currency part of the trade.
 Why is that?
 Confusion is good, you learn from that.
 And this can be very confusing, I know.
 What is this equation trying to do?
 We are trying to make the specter returns the same.
 That's the whole idea of this.
 So if I am now telling you that one bond is paying a higher interest than the other one,
 I need to offset that somehow. How do I offset it by expecting a depreciation of the bond that is
 denominated in the currency that is expected to depreciate? So what I need to do is compensate
 say, for the interest rate differential
 with an expected depreciation of the currency that's
 paying a higher interest rate.
 So that's what, in this model, when
 I fix the expected exchange rate,
 the only way I can do that is by appreciating the currency today
 so I can expect it to depreciate in the future.

 You lost the trade.
 What about an increase in the foreign interest rate,
 i star?
 So an increase in the foreign interest rate,
 let's start from the same situation we had before.
 We start from interest rate equal to international interest
 rate, therefore, the exchange rate
 is equal to expected exchange rate.
 And now, the foreign interest rate goes up.
 What is going on now in the US?
 The US is sort of stabilizing here,
 and Europe is beginning to hike a little more than the US.
 So we know from the equation that that means the exchange
 rate will fall, that is, will drop here.
 So that means the exchange rate is depreciating.
 and the dollar is depreciating.
 Why is the dollar depreciating?
 Yeah, that's correct.
 I mean, the issue here in terms of the economics
 is that, remember, if we start from the same interest rate
 and now all the lines that I'm giving you
 doesn't need to start from the same interest rate.

[G00024]  It's simpler to start from the same interest.
 But suppose we start with the same interest rate
 and now we increase this one, then
 that means the foreign bond is playing a higher interest
 rate than the domestic bond.
 I need to equalize the expected returns.
 The only way I can do that is by having an expected
 appreciation of the dollar.
 Since the expected exchange, if we fix it here, the only way
 I can give you an expected appreciation of the dollar is
 by depreciating the dollar today.
 So it's the same mechanism, the same logic, it's symmetric.
 That's the mechanism.
 Now, is this true in the very short run?
 When i star goes up and i doesn't move, then lots of
 People go and buy foreign bonds, and that produces demand
 for euros and blah, blah, blah, blah.
 But that's very quick.
 Machines do it for you now.
 It happens very quickly.
 So this equation shows you what happens after all that mess
 has already clear, which happens in milliseconds now.

[G00024]  It's simpler to start from the same interest.
 But suppose we start with the same interest rate
 and now we increase this one, then
 that means the foreign bond is playing a higher interest
 rate than the domestic bond.
 I need to equalize the expected returns.
 The only way I can do that is by having an expected
 appreciation of the dollar.
 Since the expected exchange, if we fix it here, the only way
 I can give you an expected appreciation of the dollar is
 by depreciating the dollar today.
 So it's the same mechanism, the same logic, it's symmetric.
 That's the mechanism.
 Now, is this true in the very short run?
 When i star goes up and i doesn't move, then lots of
 People go and buy foreign bonds, and that produces demand
 for euros and blah, blah, blah, blah.
 But that's very quick.
 Machines do it for you now.
 It happens very quickly.
 So this equation shows you what happens after all that mess
 has already clear, which happens in milliseconds now.

chunk.text_content:
[G00025]  What if I change the expected exchange rate?
 So again, I'm fixing it, but I can move it around.
 I'm treating it as a parameter.
 When I fix it, I just don't want to endogenize it.
 I don't want to make it another endogenous variable.
 So what happens here is we start with the same situation
 we had before, now the spectral exchanger goes up.
 Well, from the equation, it's very clear.
 The current exchange immediately rises.
 One for one, in fact.
 If I have these two interests, they are the same.
 And now I move the spectral exchange rate up,
 then the current exchange immediately jumps.
 So if we expect the dollar to appreciate in the future,
 then it appreciates today.
 Why is that? Expectations are very powerful in financial assets in general.
 This is the first time you come and we'll talk a lot more about that in the next week,
 but you can see it here. So if I move the exchange rate today up, the expected exchange rate,
 means we expect the exchange rate to be, you know, today the dollar is 90 cents on,
 90 cent, 0.9 euros per dollar.

[G00025]  What if I change the expected exchange rate?
 So again, I'm fixing it, but I can move it around.
 I'm treating it as a parameter.
 When I fix it, I just don't want to endogenize it.
 I don't want to make it another endogenous variable.
 So what happens here is we start with the same situation
 we had before, now the spectral exchanger goes up.
 Well, from the equation, it's very clear.
 The current exchange immediately rises.
 One for one, in fact.
 If I have these two interests, they are the same.
 And now I move the spectral exchange rate up,
 then the current exchange immediately jumps.
 So if we expect the dollar to appreciate in the future,
 then it appreciates today.
 Why is that? Expectations are very powerful in financial assets in general.
 This is the first time you come and we'll talk a lot more about that in the next week,
 but you can see it here. So if I move the exchange rate today up, the expected exchange rate,
 means we expect the exchange rate to be, you know, today the dollar is 90 cents on,
 90 cent, 0.9 euros per dollar.

[G00026]  Well, suppose I expect 1 euro for dollar in the next period.
 What will happen to exchange today?
 Well, it jumps today to 1.
 Why is that?
 That's your friend, the trader there.
 But yes, that's true.
 That's true.
 What does that mean, though?
 It is true, it's more expensive, but why did you want to buy it to start with?
 I mean, who cares that something is more expensive if you are not trying to buy it?
 Because the current price of something also has to take into account its future price.
 That's what the question says, yes?
 Because it's valued at the present moment, takes into account so much value in the future.
 You know, this is an arbitrage-type relationship.

 Now the spectral exchanger went up by 10%, say.

[G00028]  What do you do?
 Which bond do you buy?
 I love it.
 Of course, because you have a 10% expected capital gain
 from buying that bond, if that doesn't happen.
 The two bonds are paying the same interest rate.
 And now I tell you, well, yeah, but one is going to appreciate
 by 10% relative to the other.
 So clearly, you go short massively the foreign bond,
 and you go very long the US bond.
 That's what you do.
 We all want to do the same.
 So it happens very quickly.
 And the exchanges appreciate today
 up to a point in which that incentive is no longer there.
 And in this particular case, if the interests are the same,
 that will happen only if the exchange rate
 jumps exactly by the same amount as the expected value
 of the dollar change in the future.
 Think about this.
 Play with these things.
 I know it can be confusing.
 And I always start with, let me move something.

[G00029]  The equation tells me this has to happen
 to exchange it, well, suppose that didn't happen to exchange it.
 And then you say, oh, then I clearly invest in this bond.
 This dominates the other one.
 Well, that condition tells you, no, no.
 In equilibrium, you have to be indifferent.
 So the only thing that can move is exchange rate.
 And exchange rate has to move until you're indifferent again
 after you have done some argument
 on the right-hand side.
 That's the way you need to think about it.
 So here, I'm just plotting this relationship
 in the space of exchange rate in the x-axis
 and the domestic interest rate here.
 So that's an upward-sloping relation.
 You can see here, as I move the interest rate up or the other
 way around.
 But anyways, if I move the interest rate up,
 the exchange rate is going up.
 So that's a positive relationship.
 I can do it the other way around.

[G00030]  as they move the exchange rate up,
 then the domestic interest rate has to go up.
 I'm taking as parameters the foreign interest rate
 and the expected exchange rate.
 I take as parameter this and that,
 then I have a positive relationship
 between the exchange rate and the domestic interest rate.
 So that's going to be the ui.
 I'm plotting the ui p and covering interest parity
 condition.
 Notice this point here is interesting.
 This point tells you that when the domestic interest rate,
 if i is equal to international interest rate,
 then the exchange rate has to be equal to the expected
 exchange rate, which is the question I asked before.
 Remember, I asked you a question.
 Well, suppose that we start with an interest rate that
 is equal to the international interest rate, what
 is the exchange rate?
 And you said the answer was, well,
 it has to be equal to the expected exchange rate.
 That's that point here.

[G00029]  The equation tells me this has to happen
 to exchange it, well, suppose that didn't happen to exchange it.
 And then you say, oh, then I clearly invest in this bond.
 This dominates the other one.
 Well, that condition tells you, no, no.
 In equilibrium, you have to be indifferent.
 So the only thing that can move is exchange rate.
 And exchange rate has to move until you're indifferent again
 after you have done some argument
 on the right-hand side.
 That's the way you need to think about it.
 So here, I'm just plotting this relationship
 in the space of exchange rate in the x-axis
 and the domestic interest rate here.
 So that's an upward-sloping relation.
 You can see here, as I move the interest rate up or the other
 way around.
 But anyways, if I move the interest rate up,
 the exchange rate is going up.
 So that's a positive relationship.
 I can do it the other way around.

[G00030]  as they move the exchange rate up,
 then the domestic interest rate has to go up.
 I'm taking as parameters the foreign interest rate
 and the expected exchange rate.
 I take as parameter this and that,
 then I have a positive relationship
 between the exchange rate and the domestic interest rate.
 So that's going to be the ui.
 I'm plotting the ui p and covering interest parity
 condition.
 Notice this point here is interesting.
 This point tells you that when the domestic interest rate,
 if i is equal to international interest rate,
 then the exchange rate has to be equal to the expected
 exchange rate, which is the question I asked before.
 Remember, I asked you a question.
 Well, suppose that we start with an interest rate that
 is equal to the international interest rate, what
 is the exchange rate?
 And you said the answer was, well,
 it has to be equal to the expected exchange rate.
 That's that point here.

[G00030]  as they move the exchange rate up,
 then the domestic interest rate has to go up.
 I'm taking as parameters the foreign interest rate
 and the expected exchange rate.
 I take as parameter this and that,
 then I have a positive relationship
 between the exchange rate and the domestic interest rate.
 So that's going to be the ui.
 I'm plotting the ui p and covering interest parity
 condition.
 Notice this point here is interesting.
 This point tells you that when the domestic interest rate,
 if i is equal to international interest rate,
 then the exchange rate has to be equal to the expected
 exchange rate, which is the question I asked before.
 Remember, I asked you a question.
 Well, suppose that we start with an interest rate that
 is equal to the international interest rate, what
 is the exchange rate?
 And you said the answer was, well,
 it has to be equal to the expected exchange rate.
 That's that point here.

chunk.text_content:
[G00031]  If the domestic interest rate is above that,
 the international interest rate, then the exchange rate today
 has to be above the expected exchange rate,
 because that will give you a expected depreciation
 of the currency, which will compensate for the fact
 that the domestic bond is paying a higher interest
 rate than international bond.
 Conversely, if the domestic bond is paying a lower interest
 rate, then the exchange rate today is very depreciated,
 because you have to expect it to appreciate in order
 to compensate for the interest rate differential.
 Probably not, but this requires practice, I tell you.
 OK, but now we have an equation for the exchanger, at least.
 So I can go back to my IS, is the IS equation
 in the open economy, and I will have an equation
 for the exchange, so I can replace it.
 This is nice, because I have two new parameters, expected
 exchange rate and international interest rate,
 but now this is also a function of the interest rate.

[G00031]  If the domestic interest rate is above that,
 the international interest rate, then the exchange rate today
 has to be above the expected exchange rate,
 because that will give you a expected depreciation
 of the currency, which will compensate for the fact
 that the domestic bond is paying a higher interest
 rate than international bond.
 Conversely, if the domestic bond is paying a lower interest
 rate, then the exchange rate today is very depreciated,
 because you have to expect it to appreciate in order
 to compensate for the interest rate differential.
 Probably not, but this requires practice, I tell you.
 OK, but now we have an equation for the exchanger, at least.
 So I can go back to my IS, is the IS equation
 in the open economy, and I will have an equation
 for the exchange, so I can replace it.
 This is nice, because I have two new parameters, expected
 exchange rate and international interest rate,
 but now this is also a function of the interest rate.

chunk.text_content:
[G00032]  So at this moment, I have one equation and two unknowns,
 really, after I solve out for the exchanges.
 I have one equation and two unknowns.
 The two unknowns are its output and the domestic interest rate.
 All the rest are parameters.
 So that's the same situation we're at in lecture three
 or so.
 So then we need an extra equation.
 The extra equation was monetary policy, the LM.
 We're going to do exactly the same here.
 The LM is the same.
 It's a domestic central bank, sets the interest rate.
 So now I'm set.
 Now we have the ISLM model in the open economy.
 This is the Mandel Fleming model.
 That's what the Mandel Fleming model is.
 So yes, a more complicated I.S. with a U.I.P. driven exchange
 rate, and then the L.M. is the same as in the closed economy.
 So this is the Mandel Fleming law.
 So one thing we know already, we knew from the previous
 lecture, that we have a smaller multiply in the open
 economy, because we have the imports that are also
 responding to out.

[G00032]  So at this moment, I have one equation and two unknowns,
 really, after I solve out for the exchanges.
 I have one equation and two unknowns.
 The two unknowns are its output and the domestic interest rate.
 All the rest are parameters.
 So that's the same situation we're at in lecture three
 or so.
 So then we need an extra equation.
 The extra equation was monetary policy, the LM.
 We're going to do exactly the same here.
 The LM is the same.
 It's a domestic central bank, sets the interest rate.
 So now I'm set.
 Now we have the ISLM model in the open economy.
 This is the Mandel Fleming model.
 That's what the Mandel Fleming model is.
 So yes, a more complicated I.S. with a U.I.P. driven exchange
 rate, and then the L.M. is the same as in the closed economy.
 So this is the Mandel Fleming law.
 So one thing we know already, we knew from the previous
 lecture, that we have a smaller multiply in the open
 economy, because we have the imports that are also
 responding to out.

[G00034]  So more of the domestic consumption
 is diverted to foreign goods.
 unless a foreign demand is allocated to our exports, okay?
 So that's the second channel.
 So in an open economy, and the smallest economy,
 the more important is this term, the more powerful is that channel.
 The US cares very little about this effect.
 Most other economies care a lot about this effect, okay?
 Because the US is a relatively close economy, believe it or not.
 So this is sort of the star diagram of the Mandel-Flaming model.
 So this thing here is our old ISLM model.
 It's just that this IS is a little thicker now.
 It has net exports in there and so on,
 but it looks exactly the same.
 That is, plots equilibrium in financial and goods market,
 the combinations of output and domestic interest rate
 that are consistent with equilibrium in both markets.
 That's the case here.
 This is the IS, which is all the combinations
 of domestic output and domestic interest rate
 that are consistent with equilibrium in goods market.

[G00035]  This is the interest rate that is consistent
 with equilibrium in financial markets.
 That's what the Fed does in the US.
 That point is where both markets are in equilibrium.
 But we can take this interest rate.
 So that's what will happen.
 The interest rate will be in the US.
 The interest rate is set by the Fed, not by the ECB.
 The Fed will set the interest rate.
 That will give us some equilibrium output.
 And then we can go to the UIP condition you see I'm plotting
 here and figure out what the exchange rate is.
 Because for this interest rate here, there's going to be some
 point in the UIP, and that tells me exactly what the
 exchange rate is.
 So with this set of diagrams, I can determine the interest
 rate, output, and exchange rate.
 So I can study the effects of different policies, for
 example, on output, the interest rate, of course.
 that's the policy itself, and exchange rate.

[G00036]  So this is the new thing I can explain.
 I can do a little bit of asset pricing here.
 I can explain the behavior of the exchange rate as well.
 So this diagram, I mean, you need
 to really control very, very well.
 So I'm going to play with it quite a bit.
 Monetary policy, let's do monetary policy.
 We talk about monetary policy already.
 So suppose that for whatever reason,
 Then the domestic economy, the domestic central bank decides to hike interest rate.
 Suppose the economy was overheating, output was too high, relative to natural rate of
 output for the typical reasons why you need to raise interest rate.
 And so suppose that the domestic interest rate goes up.
 Well, as it used to be, that's going to be contractionary.
 What happens to exchange rate?
 Well, I know the interest rate went up.
 I go, I look into my UIP for the high interest rate,
 and in a current exchange rate, it's above,
 they all, it has to go up, relatively tall.

[G00035]  This is the interest rate that is consistent
 with equilibrium in financial markets.
 That's what the Fed does in the US.
 That point is where both markets are in equilibrium.
 But we can take this interest rate.
 So that's what will happen.
 The interest rate will be in the US.
 The interest rate is set by the Fed, not by the ECB.
 The Fed will set the interest rate.
 That will give us some equilibrium output.
 And then we can go to the UIP condition you see I'm plotting
 here and figure out what the exchange rate is.
 Because for this interest rate here, there's going to be some
 point in the UIP, and that tells me exactly what the
 exchange rate is.
 So with this set of diagrams, I can determine the interest
 rate, output, and exchange rate.
 So I can study the effects of different policies, for
 example, on output, the interest rate, of course.
 that's the policy itself, and exchange rate.

[G00036]  So this is the new thing I can explain.
 I can do a little bit of asset pricing here.
 I can explain the behavior of the exchange rate as well.
 So this diagram, I mean, you need
 to really control very, very well.
 So I'm going to play with it quite a bit.
 Monetary policy, let's do monetary policy.
 We talk about monetary policy already.
 So suppose that for whatever reason,
 Then the domestic economy, the domestic central bank decides to hike interest rate.
 Suppose the economy was overheating, output was too high, relative to natural rate of
 output for the typical reasons why you need to raise interest rate.
 And so suppose that the domestic interest rate goes up.
 Well, as it used to be, that's going to be contractionary.
 What happens to exchange rate?
 Well, I know the interest rate went up.
 I go, I look into my UIP for the high interest rate,
 and in a current exchange rate, it's above,
 they all, it has to go up, relatively tall.

[G00037]  When I increase interest rate from here to there,
 then my exchange rate has to appreciate.
 Why is that?
 So an expansionary domestic monetary policy will lead
 to a contraction in output, which is what we get
 out of monetary policy, but it will also
 lead to an appreciation of the currency.
 Why is that?
 That's what we just discussed.
 It's UAP.
 If I move the domestic interest rate,
 and the rest of the world does not follow me,
 so we move interest rate dead on,
 then now I need to compensate for this increase
 in the interest rate differential.
 And the compensation will come through an expected capital
 loss through the currency.
 So if I appreciate more of the currencies and I haven't moved the expected exchange rate,
 I expect a larger loss from the currency side.
 That's what has happened here.
 That's what is behind the precision.
 And of course, the precision is already built in here, which is what makes monetary policy
 more powerful than the close economy, because you get the next export channel.

[G00038]  But that's built in here.
 OK, here, all that I did is exactly the same as we were
 doing in the last 30 minutes.
 I just used this UIP.
 For whatever domestic reason, I need to raise interest rate,
 have contractual and monetary policy.
 Well, one of the effects that you're going to get in an
 open economy is that your currency will
 tend to appreciate.
 What about fiscal policy?
 Well, if the Fed doesn't follow, if the central bank
 doesn't follow, and you have an expansionary fiscal policy,
 then that will increase output.
 It has no effect on the interest rate.
 Therefore, it has absolutely no effect on the exchange rate.
 So an expansionary fiscal policy,
 which is accumulated by the Fed,
 that means the interest rate is kept at the same level,
 then does not lead to an appreciation of the currency.
 It doesn't move the exchange rate.
 It has no implication for the exchange rate.
 Now, what about this change in output?

[G00039]  Is it larger or smaller than the one we did in lecture 3 or 4?
 Smaller, why?
 Exactly, because it goes to import.
 OK, good.
 So this is smaller than it was in the close economy,
 but it has no impact on the exchange rate.
 That is, the UAP has nothing to do with government expenditure.
 It's all about financial markets.
 It's about expected returns, things like that.
 So unless the fiscal policy somehow affects interest rate,
 then there is no effect.
 What may happen is that, for example,
 is that treasury becomes very expansionary,
 and this output becomes too large for what
 is consistent with a zero output gap or no inflation.
 And then the Fed may react and raise interest rate,
 and that will lead to a conversation of exchanges
 and so on.
 And that's the reason why, in practice,
 when countries have sort of expansionary fiscal packages,
 the currency tends to appreciate it.
 It's because investors expect the Fed to react to that,
 or the central bank to react to that and raise interest rates.

[G00037]  When I increase interest rate from here to there,
 then my exchange rate has to appreciate.
 Why is that?
 So an expansionary domestic monetary policy will lead
 to a contraction in output, which is what we get
 out of monetary policy, but it will also
 lead to an appreciation of the currency.
 Why is that?
 That's what we just discussed.
 It's UAP.
 If I move the domestic interest rate,
 and the rest of the world does not follow me,
 so we move interest rate dead on,
 then now I need to compensate for this

[G00037] increase
 in the interest rate differential.
 And the compensation will come through an expected capital
 loss through the currency.
 So if I appreciate more of the currencies and I haven't moved the expected exchange rate,
 I expect a larger loss from the currency side.
 That's what has happened here.
 That's what is behind the precision.
 And of course, the precision is already built in here, which is what makes monetary policy
 more powerful than the close economy, because you get the next export channel.

[G00038]  But that's built in here.
 OK, here, all that I did is exactly the same as we were
 doing in the last 30 minutes.
 I just used this UIP.
 For whatever domestic reason, I need to raise interest rate,
 have contractual and monetary policy.
 Well, one of the effects that you're going to get in an
 open economy is that your currency will
 tend to appreciate.
 What about fiscal policy?
 Well, if the Fed doesn't follow, if the central bank
 doesn't follow, and you have an expansionary fiscal policy,
 then that will increase output.
 It has no effect on the interest rate.
 Therefore, it has absolutely no effect on the exchange rate.
 So an expansionary fiscal policy,
 which is accumulated by the Fed,
 that means the interest rate is kept at the same level,
 then does not lead to an appreciation of the currency.
 It doesn't move the exchange rate.
 It has no implication for the exchange rate.
 Now, what about this change in output?

[G00039]  Is it larger or smaller than the one we did in lecture 3 or 4?
 Smaller, why?
 Exactly, because it goes to import.
 OK, good.
 So this is smaller than it was in the close economy,
 but it has no impact on the exchange rate.
 That is, the UAP has nothing to do with government expenditure.
 It's all about financial markets.
 It's about expected returns, things like that.
 So unless the fiscal policy somehow affects interest rate,
 then there is no effect.
 What may happen is that, for example,
 is that treasury becomes very expansionary,
 and this output becomes too large for what
 is consistent with a zero output gap or no inflation.
 And then the Fed may react and raise interest rate,
 and that will lead to a conversation of exchanges
 and so on.
 And that's the reason why, in practice,
 when countries have sort of expansionary fiscal packages,
 the currency tends to appreciate it.
 It's because investors expect the Fed to react to that,
 or the central bank to react to that and raise interest rates.

chunk.text_content:
[G00039]  Is it larger or smaller than the one we did in lecture 3 or 4?
 Smaller, why?
 Exactly, because it goes to import.
 OK, good.
 So this is smaller than it was in the close economy,
 but it has no impact on the exchange rate.
 That is, the UAP has nothing to do with government expenditure.
 It's all about financial markets.
 It's about expected returns, things like that.
 So unless the fiscal policy somehow affects interest rate,
 then there is no effect.
 What may happen is that, for example,
 is that treasury becomes very expansionary,
 and this output becomes too large for what
 is consistent with a zero output gap or no inflation.
 And then the Fed may react and raise interest rate,
 and that will lead to a conversation of exchanges
 and so on.
 And that's the reason why, in practice,
 when countries have sort of expansionary fiscal packages,
 the currency tends to appreciate it.
 It's because investors expect the Fed to react to that,
 or the central bank to react to that and raise interest rates.

[G00040]  But if the Fed says, no, no, we need that fiscal expansion,
 I'm not going to move the interest rate,
 then the exchange rate won't move.
 So let's use a little more of this model
 and look at other shocks within this model.
 So let's start with, suppose that we increase the expected exchange rate, what
 moves in this diagram? Let's go, does the LEM move? The LEM is controlled by domestic central bank, does it move?
 Does the IES move? When I ask you whether it moves, you should always fix something. So you say, okay, let me fix the interest rate.
 say, pick a point, like this one, say.
 And now I have to ask the question, what happens to
 output now that I have moved the expected exchange rate?
 If I get the same output back, it means that
 the S has a move.
 If I get a different output, equilibrium output, then I
 find out that the S did move.

[G00041]  So what is the answer?
 If the interest rate doesn't move, the foreign interest
 doesn't move, and the expected exchange rate goes
 up, what happens to the current exchange rate?
 Appreciate.
 What happens when there's an appreciation?
 Net exports decline.
 That means that moves the yes to the left.
 So this movement will move the yes to the left
 as a first effect.
 What about the UIP condition? Will it move or not?
 We are taking that as a parameter.
 Will it move?
 I mean, remember, I give you a clue because I said
 we are taking these two as parameters here.
 So if I move a parameter, most likely, I will move the current.
 But in which direction will it move?
 To the right.
 Yes, because for the same interest rate,
 now I need the exchange rate to move one for one,
 the current exchange rate to move one for one,
 with the expected exchange rate.
 So this was the exchange rate before.

[G00042]  And now the expected exchange rate moved to the right.
 Well, in order not to generate expected capital gain or loss,
 Because I have to move the current exchange rate
 by the same amount.
 And so that means this curve will shift to the right.
 What if I move for an output?
 Down.
 What happens?
 Which curve moves?
 Well, this is not a parameter here, so this is not moving.
 This is not a parameter here, so this one is not moving.
 Only one can move.
 Yes, where?
 It will move to the left, because net exports will decline.
 Not for any given level of the interest rate,
 now we're going to have less net exports.
 And therefore, the US moves to the left, so output falls.
 But there's no movement here.
 Unless the Fed reacts to that, the central bank reacts to that,
 it won't happen.
 And it may well be the case that you want to react to that.

[G00043]  If the whole world goes into a recession,
 the US is very likely to lower interest rates,
 Because it's very contractionary.
 The whole world goes into recession.
 When the US goes into recession, the rest of the
 world, everyone wants to cut interest rates because the US
 is a big player.
 So it really drags everyone down.
 Good.
 The last one, and I'm going to repeat this in the next
 lecture, is, well, what happens if a star moves up?
 Foreign interest rate moves up.
 Well, the land doesn't move.
 move, this one will move, which way?
 Because that was a parameter here.
 To the right?
 You said to the right.
 That's right.
 So I think what happened here, if the foreign interest rate
 goes up at any given interest rate,
 now the domestic bond is doing worse than otherwise.
 twice.
 So I need to depreciate the exchange rate today
 in order to expect an appreciation.
 That means this curve moves to the left.

[G00041]  So what is the answer?
 If the interest rate doesn't move, the foreign interest
 doesn't move, and the expected exchange rate goes
 up, what happens to the current exchange rate?
 Appreciate.
 What happens when there's an appreciation?
 Net exports decline.
 That means that moves the yes to the left.
 So this movement will move the yes to the left
 as a first effect.
 What about the UIP condition? Will it move or not?
 We are taking that as a parameter.
 Will it move?
 I mean, remember, I give you a clue because I said
 we are taking these two as parameters here.
 So if I move a parameter, most likely, I will move the current.
 But in which direction will it move?
 To the right.
 Yes, because for the same interest rate,
 now I need the exchange rate to move one for one,
 the current exchange rate to move one for one,
 with the expected exchange rate.
 So this was the exchange rate before.

[G00042]  And now the expected exchange rate moved to the right.
 Well, in order not to generate expected capital gain or loss,
 Because I have to move the current exchange rate
 by the same amount.
 And so that means this curve will shift to the right.
 What if I move for an output?
 Down.
 What happens?
 Which curve moves?
 Well, this is not a parameter here, so this is not moving.
 This is not a parameter here, so this one is not moving.
 Only one can move.
 Yes, where?
 It will move to the left, because net exports will decline.
 Not for any given level of the interest rate,
 now we're going to have less net exports.
 And therefore, the US moves to the left, so output falls.
 But there's no movement here.
 Unless the Fed reacts to that, the central bank reacts to that,
 it won't happen.
 And it may well be the case that you want to react to that.

[G00043]  If the whole world goes into a recession,
 the US is very likely to lower interest rates,
 Because it's very contractionary.
 The whole world goes into recession.
 When the US goes into recession, the rest of the
 world, everyone wants to cut interest rates because the US
 is a big player.
 So it really drags everyone down.
 Good.
 The last one, and I'm going to repeat this in the next
 lecture, is, well, what happens if a star moves up?
 Foreign interest rate moves up.
 Well, the land doesn't move.
 move, this one will move, which way?
 Because that was a parameter here.
 To the right?
 You said to the right.
 That's right.
 So I think what happened here, if the foreign interest rate
 goes up at any given interest rate,
 now the domestic bond is doing worse than otherwise.
 twice.
 So I need to depreciate the exchange rate today
 in order to expect an appreciation.
 That means this curve moves to the left.
